attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post. He reports the AAAI survey result and endorses it with 'They were right.'

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the survey, the 'vast majority of academic AI researchers' scope, 'all the way to AGI' and the endorsement. Filing it as an observation works because it is a retrospective, settled judgment, although the endorsement half is hard to test.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: 'vast majority' means a clear supermajority, and 'They were right' means scaling really is insufficient, not just that one model fell short. Both halves have to be checked, and the result depends on how 'right' is read.

evidence.note: Contemporaneous report: 76% of respondents rated scaling current systems to AGI unlikely or very unlikely. This supports the survey half. It gives no academic-only figure and says nothing on whether the doubts were correct.

AAAI describing its own survey: 67% of respondents gave academia as their main affiliation. That roughly backs 'academic researchers' as a description of the sample, but there is no academic-only breakdown.
Shows the report was public by March 7, 2025, before the post. Background on availability only.
September 2026 benchmark post: ARC Prize says Astra shows major progress but does not claim it is AGI. This neither shows AGI was reached by scaling nor shows scaling is insufficient.

reviews.rationale: The survey half largely holds: 76% of respondents, about two-thirds of them academics, doubted that scaling would reach AGI. That is a clear supermajority, though there is no academic-only figure. The endorsement half ('They were right') needs evidence that scaling really is insufficient, and the packet has none. It also has no demonstration of AGI through scaling that would contradict him. Since the contract requires both halves, the overall result is unresolved, with the survey report supported.
